passage: Ishita, you asked why I, Seema, stopped eating meat last year when nobody at home did. It wasn't a rule from anyone. I'd read about how animals are raised, and I kept thinking about it at dinner. At first I just tried it for a month. Then I read more, argued with my cousins, even changed my mind twice. My family thought it was a phase. But I've kept going, and now it feels like mine, not borrowed. I still go to the temple with Nani, and I still ask her hard questions on the way. She says questioning is part of believing. I think she's right. I'm sixteen, and I'm still working out the rest.

qa.q: What did Seema try for a month first?
qa.a: Not eating meat.

qa.q: How does Seema feel about the choice now?
qa.a: Seema feels settled and sure, saying it now feels her own, not borrowed.

qa.q: What would you advise Seema as she keeps exploring her beliefs?
qa.a: Keep reading and talking with people Seema trusts, like Nani, and stay open to changing her mind again.

qa.q: How might Nani see Seema's hard questions?
qa.a: Nani seems to welcome them, seeing questioning as part of real belief.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring and committing to a personal belief while still questioning her family's faith.

passage: I'm Preeti, Jahnavi's younger sister. Last year Jahnavi, who's sixteen, started going to Saturday meetings of a youth group that cleans up the lake and talks about water rights. At first she came home and argued with Papa about the factory upstream. Papa said she was too young to understand. She went quiet, then came back a week later with printed reports and asked him to read them. Now she has a notebook of what she believes and why, with some pages crossed out. I don't know how deep it goes for her, but she hasn't missed a Saturday.

qa.q: What does the youth group clean up?
qa.a: The lake.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have felt when Papa said she was too young?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated and hurt, but also determined to prove her view with evidence.

qa.q: How could Jahnavi keep talking with Papa without it becoming a fight?
qa.a: Share her sources calmly and ask to hear his reasons, so they can discuss rather than argue.

qa.q: How does Preeti see Jahnavi's new commitment?
qa.a: Preeti isn't sure how deep it goes, but notices Jahnavi hasn't missed a single Saturday.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring and committing to a set of beliefs about the environment, seen by her younger sister.

passage: March: Arnab, sixteen, and his friend Jeevan argued about whether sixteen-year-olds should vote. Arnab said yes, loudly, without really knowing why. April: after a class debate, he read both sides and realised he'd only listened to people who agreed with him. He wrote his reasons down, and some of them didn't hold up. May: he still wasn't sure about voting at sixteen, but he'd decided what mattered to him: that people know their rights. He signed up to help older neighbours check their names on the voter list. "You changed your mind," said Jeevan. "No," said Arnab. "I made it up properly this time."

qa.q: What did Arnab sign up to help with?
qa.a: Helping older neighbours check their names on the voter list.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when he realised he'd only listened to people who agreed with him?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and a bit embarrassed, which pushed him to think again.

qa.q: What made Arnab's final choice stronger than his first opinion?
qa.a: He weighed both sides, tested his reasons in writing and chose something concrete to act on.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see Arnab's change?
qa.a: He might be surprised and even respect how seriously Arnab thought it through.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring political beliefs over months and committing to what matters to him.

passage:
Uma's diary, Friday
Career day at school. My brother Darshan says I should do engineering "because you're good at maths". I'm okay at maths. But today, at the architecture stall, I couldn't stop looking at the model of a school with a courtyard. I made a list tonight. Strengths: drawing, patience, noticing small things, okay maths. Things I love: buildings, little kids. Things I hate: sitting still for hours. So maybe architecture. Or maybe teaching. Maybe something that mixes both, like designing schools? I'm fifteen, so I don't have to decide yet, but it felt good to think about it properly.

qa.q: How might Darshan react to Uma's list?
qa.a: Darshan might be surprised, but could respect that Uma is choosing based on real strengths.

grounding: Shows a teenager imagining career paths and weighing personal strengths against them.

passage: Eshaan, sixteen, came back from the village school in a foul mood and snapped at his little sister Charu when she asked for help with her maths. She went quiet and did it alone. That night, lying on the charpai under the stars, he thought about his own older cousin, who used to shout at him and whom he still avoided at weddings. He didn't want to be that. The next morning he sat beside Charu at breakfast. "Sorry about yesterday. Show me the sums." She blinked, then pushed the notebook over. He decided then: he would be the brother she could come to.

passage: In Amsterdam, Sami, fifteen, heard that his friend Yosef's parents were splitting up. Yosef hadn't said a word; he'd just stopped coming to football. Sami thought about the friends who'd drifted away when his own grandfather died, and the one who'd kept showing up with bad jokes and snacks. He knew which one he wanted to be. So on Saturday he cycled to Yosef's flat with a bag of crisps. "You don't have to talk," he said. They played video games for three hours in near silence. Before Sami left, Yosef said, "Come next week?"

qa.q: What did Sami bring to Yosef's flat?
qa.a: A bag of crisps.

qa.q: What was Sami thinking about when he decided to visit?
qa.a: He remembered feeling hurt by friends who drifted away and grateful for the one who stayed, and wanted to be like that one.

qa.q: How might Yosef feel when Sami says he doesn't have to talk?

passage: In the college hostel, Nilesh, seventeen, overheard two boys laughing about his roommate Raghav's accent and his old phone. One of them turned to Nilesh. "You share a room with him, right? Tell us something funny." Nilesh felt the pull to join in, to be one of them. He also remembered how Raghav had stayed up to help him with physics. "Nothing funny," he said. "He's a good roommate." The boys shrugged and moved on. Back in the room, Nilesh didn't mention it. But he realised he'd just decided something about the kind of friend he wanted to be.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when the boys asked him for something funny?

passage:
Counsellor's note, Alka, August
Abhinav (14) was referred by three teachers for disrupting class. In our session, he admitted he makes jokes during lessons because it gets laughs from the older boys he wants to be friends with. "If I'm quiet, I'm invisible," he said. He isn't malicious; he's lonely and trying to rise in the group. We talked about other ways to be noticed: he's good at drawing and quick with ideas. passage: I'm Devika. In Class 10 my whole group chose science. Everyone assumed I would too. I love history, the old maps, the stories behind the dates, but I didn't say anything for weeks. At lunch they'd plan who would sit together in physics. I nodded along. My friend Ishita finally asked, "Why do you look sad every time we talk about this?" I told her. She didn't laugh. She said, "Then pick history. I'll still sit with you at lunch." I did. Some of the others stopped inviting me. Ishita didn't. I still think about how close I came to choosing their future instead of mine.

qa.q: What subject does Devika love?
qa.a: History.

qa.q: How did Devika feel while nodding along to the science plans?
qa.a: Devika felt sad and trapped, hiding what she really wanted to fit in.

qa.q: What would you advise someone in Devika's position?
qa.a: Talk to one trusted friend or adult early, as Devika eventually did with Ishita.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt watching Devika during those weeks?
qa.a: Concerned and puzzled, sensing something was wrong behind the nodding.

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing a personal path over the pressure to follow friends' subject choices.

passage: In the Delhi school staffroom, Manjula Ma'am handed back Rukmini's essay covered in red. "Your argument is strong, but your evidence is thin. And paragraph three repeats paragraph one." passage: In the small town, Devika, sixteen, practised Bharatanatyam every morning before school on the flat roof, while the rest of the house slept. Her teacher Shalini had said she had the steps but not yet the feeling. So Devika watched old performances in the evenings and cried at one of them without knowing why. She started practising the facial expressions in front of the steel almirah's mirror. Her feet bled once. She didn't stop. When Shalini finally said, "Now you're telling the story," Devika felt her whole chest open. She wanted this more than anything.

qa.q: Where did Devika practise every morning?
qa.a: On the flat roof.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when Shalini said she was telling the story?
qa.a: She felt overjoyed and moved, as if her whole chest opened.

qa.q: What would you advise Devika about her bleeding feet?
qa.a: Rest and have them looked at by an adult, since passion lasts longer when the body is cared for.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Devika's progress?
qa.a: With pride, seeing a student who went beyond steps to real feeling.

grounding: Shows a teenager's intense emotional investment in classical dance.

passage:
"So? You made the team list?" asked his cousin Thomas.
"Didn't check," said Sahil, fifteen, scrolling his phone.
"It went up at noon."
"Whatever. Cricket's boring anyway."
"You practised every day for two months."
"So? I was bored."
Thomas sat beside him. "Your name's not on it. I saw."
Sahil's thumb stopped over the screen. For a while the only sound was the ceiling fan. "I know."
"You can be upset."
"I'm not."
"Okay." Thomas waited.
After a long moment, Sahil put the phone face down on the bed. His voice came out smaller than he wanted. "I really thought I'd make it. I even told Nani I would." Thomas nudged his shoulder. "Trials come again in March." Sahil didn't answer, but he didn't say 'whatever' either.

qa.q: When did the team list go up?
qa.a: At noon.

qa.q: Why did Sahil say cricket was boring?
qa.a: He was hurt and disappointed at not making the team, and pretending not to care protected him.

qa.q: What did Thomas do that helped Sahil open up?
qa.a: He stayed, named the truth gently and waited without pushing.

qa.q: How does Thomas see Sahil's "whatever"?
qa.a: He sees through it, knowing Sahil practised hard and must be disappointed.

grounding: Shows a teenager using feigned indifference to hide disappointment, and a cousin gently seeing through it.

passage: I'm Dhruv. When my best friend Gurpreet moved to Canada last year, I told everyone I didn't care. At the farewell, I made jokes and left early. When he messaged from the airport, I replied "ok". My mum asked if I was upset and I said, "People move. It's fine." But I stopped going to the ground where we used to play. It took me months to understand that acting cool was easier than admitting how much I missed him. Last week I finally called him and said, "I miss you, man." He said, "Same." It felt awful and good at once.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet move to?
qa.a: To Canada.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv act like he didn't care?
qa.a: Dhruv felt deeply sad about losing his friend, and acting cool protected him from that pain.

qa.q: What turning point helped Dhruv?
qa.a: Admitting the truth, that Dhruv missed Gurpreet, and finally calling to say so.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt when Dhruv replied "ok" from the airport?
qa.a: Probably hurt or confused, wondering if Dhruv cared at all.

grounding: Shows a teenager looking back on using detachment to hide sadness about a friend moving away.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Disha, October
Tenzin (14) was sent to me after his teacher noticed he'd stopped handing in homework. When I asked, he shrugged: "Doesn't matter. Nothing matters." He kept his arms folded, but his leg was bouncing. Later he mentioned he'd failed the trials for the school band, which he'd been preparing for all summer. The "I don't care" seems to be a shield. I didn't push. I've arranged a weekly check-in, asked the music teacher to speak with him, and will call his parents to share what I noticed.

qa.q: What trials did Tenzin fail?
qa.a: The trials for the school band.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's bouncing leg suggest despite his shrug?
qa.a: He feels more upset and anxious than he admits, using indifference as a shield.

qa.q: Why is Disha right not to push Tenzin?
qa.a: Pushing might make him defend the shield harder; steady check-ins build trust so he can open up.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's parents feel when Disha calls?
qa.a: Concerned but grateful to understand what's behind his change.

grounding: Shows a young teenager using a show of not caring to protect himself after a disappointment, noted by his counsellor.

passage: Imran, you asked why I've been so short with everyone. You know me, Anirban, the one who always had a plan? Lately I don't. Every time I open my phone it's layoffs, heatwaves, some war. My father says study hard and you'll be fine, but his office just cut half the staff. I lie awake angry at everyone and scared of nothing I can name. I snapped at my sister for breathing too loudly. That's not me. Last week I told our class teacher, and she set up a meeting with the school counsellor for Thursday. I don't expect a magic fix. I just didn't want to carry this alone any more, so I'm telling you too.

qa.q: When is Anirban's meeting with the school counsellor?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: What is Anirban feeling while lying awake at night?
qa.a: Anirban feels angry and scared at once, a general dread about the future with no single cause.

qa.q: What was a good step in Anirban's story, and what else could help?
qa.a: Telling the class teacher and a friend; cutting down late-night news on the phone could also help.

qa.q: How might Imran feel hearing all this?
qa.a: Concerned, but also trusted and glad that Anirban chose to share it.

grounding: Shows a teenager's generalised anger and dread about the world and the future, and a decision to seek support.

passage: I'm Anand, Sharmila's younger brother. This term Sharmila, who's sixteen, stays up late reading the news on her phone, and in the mornings she's snappy and tired. Last night at dinner she pushed her plate away and said, "Why study if the whole world is falling apart?" Nobody knew what to say. Amma followed her to her room and sat on the bed with her for a long time. Later Amma told us they'd agreed on no phone after ten and a visit to the school counsellor this week. This morning Sharmila put her phone on the kitchen shelf before bed. I don't know what's inside her head, but she looked a little lighter.

qa.q: What did Sharmila say at dinner?
qa.a: "Why study if the whole world is falling apart?"

qa.q: What might Sharmila be feeling when she pushes her plate away?
qa.a: She seems anxious and frustrated, weighed down by a general dread about the world.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with Sharmila, listened, and agreed on small steps: no phone after ten and a visit to the school counsellor.

qa.q: How does Anand see the change in Sharmila?
qa.a: He notices she looks a little lighter, though he admits he can't know what's inside her head.

grounding: Shows a teenager's dread about the world and her place in it, noticed by her brother, and the family's supportive response.
